newsitem.title: GERMANY: German grain trade expects EU to act on exports.
newsitem.headline: German grain trade expects EU to act on exports.

text.p: German grain traders want Brussels cereals export managers to resume subsidised exports soon, speakers at a meeting of 120 country merchants here said.
They fear new-crop prices could fall sharply if the European Union fails to restore its weekly export routine which it suspended in April to help keep domestic prices down.
"I hope the EU moves immediately, there is a big grain crop coming in and I'm not at all bullish on prices," said Detlef Schoen, of country merchants Nordland Agrarhandelsges in Demmin.
He said Morocco and Tunesia were looking for more Sept/Oct wheat which they could also buy in the United States.
The EU cereals management committee will hold its next weekly meeting on July 3.
Schoen said Poland, a typical wheat buyer in Germany, was sitting on old-crop supply while Hungary and Romania were due to harvest good crops this year which they might market abroad.
EU was expecting a broadly steady wheat crop of 90 million tonnes of which 14 million might be available for export in 1997-98 (July-June) after 10 million, excluding flour, in the 1996-97 season.
Total grain export volumes from the EU in 97-98 were put at 25-30 million tonnes.
"Each week that goes by without action might lose the EU 500,000 tonnes in lost exports," one delegate said privately.
Bread wheat prices from the new crop at roughly 280 marks were already 20 marks down from a year ago.
A Bavarian delegate said farmers, traders and industrial consumers in Germany had built siyeable stocks from the 1996 harvest of 42 million tonnes, which included 18.9 million tonnes of wheat.
German traders were anxious to participate in EU third country exports because they often had higher transport and handling costs than competing suppliers in other western European countries.
German wheat, although qualitatively high, also faced competiton from France and Britain in southern Europe.
But consumers at the meeting said the lower price would encourage domestic grain use in feed and bakery products.
